claim: Alpha-dystroglycan (α-DG) plays a major role in bridging the extracellular matrix to the muscle plasma membrane and actin cytoskeleton as a component of the multi-protein dystrophin glycoprotein complex.
source: Twenty-five years ago it was proposed that alpha-dystroglycan (α-DG) played a major role in bridging the extracellular matrix to the muscle plasma membrane and actin cytoskeleton as a component of the multi-protein dystrophin glycoprotein complex (Ervasti et al., 1990; Yoshida and Ozawa, 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Ervasti et al., 1990; Yoshida and Ozawa, 1990).

claim: Defects in the proper formation of the dystrophin glycoprotein complex have been shown to be causal for various forms of muscular dystrophy.
source: Defects in the proper formation of this complex have been shown to be causal for various forms of muscular dystrophy (Carmignac and Durbeej, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Carmignac and Durbeej, 2012.

claim: Only 3 patients have been found that have primary defects in the coding sequence of α-DG.
source: However, to date, only 3 patients have been found that have primary defects in the coding sequence of α-DG (Dong et al., 2015; Geis et al., 2013; Hara et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Dong et al., 2015; Geis et al., 2013; Hara et al., 2011).

claim: Defects in the glycosyltransferases needed for proper glycosylation of α-DG were causal for a subset of muscular dystrophies, the so-called secondary dystroglycanopathies that can range in severity from mild Limb-Girdle Muscular Dystrophy (LGMD) to severe Walker-Warburg syndrome (WWS).
source: Over fifteen years ago, it was suggested that defects in the glycosyltransferases needed for proper glycosylation of α-DG were causal for a subset of muscular dystrophies, the so-called secondary dystroglycanopathies that can range in severity from mild Limb-Girdle Muscular Dystrophy (LGMD) to severe Walker-Warburg syndrome (WWS) (Chiba et al., 1997; Holt et al., 2000; Wells, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Chiba et al., 1997; Holt et al., 2000; Wells, 2013).

claim: The defects causal for disease involved enzymes that initiated and elaborated the extended O-mannose (O-Man) glycan structures covalently attached to Ser/Thr residues of α-DG.
source: In the early 2000's, it became clear that the defects causal for disease involved enzymes that initiated and elaborated the extended O-mannose (O-Man) glycan structures covalently attached to Ser/Thr residues of α-DG (Beltrán-Valero de Bernabé et al., 2002; Michele et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Beltrán-Valero de Bernabé et al., 2002 and Michele et al., 2002.

claim: A subset of phosphorylated O-Man structures containing extended, LARGE-dependent, repeating disaccharide polymers have been recently termed matriglycan.
source: These include the identification of a subset of phosphorylated O-Man structures containing extended, LARGE-dependent, repeating disaccharide polymers, structures that have been recently termed matriglycan (Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015.

claim: The addition of O-Man in an alpha linkage to serine and threonine residues of a select set of mammalian glycoproteins is catalyzed by the POMT1/2 complex using dolichol-phosphomannose as the donor.
source: The addition of O-Man in an alpha linkage to serine and threonine residues of a select set of mammalian glycoproteins is catalyzed by the POMT1/2 complex using dolichol-phosphomannose as the donor (Beltrán-Valero de Bernabé et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Beltrán-Valero de Bernabé et al., 2002.

claim: The vast majority of O-Man sites are extended in the Golgi in a beta-1,2 linkage with N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) by POMGNT1 that can then be further branched by GlcNAc and/or elaborated by galactose, fucose, and sialic acid to generate the M1 and M2 glycans.
source: The vast majority of O-Man sites are extended in the Golgi in a beta-1,2 linkage with N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) by POMGNT1 that can then be further branched by GlcNAc and/or elaborated by galactose, fucose, and sialic acid to generate the M1 and M2 glycans (Praissman and Wells, 2014; Lee et al., 2012; Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Praissman and Wells, 2014; Lee et al., 2012; Yoshida et al., 2001.

claim: A small subset of O-Man modified sites, apparently exclusively on α-DG, are extended in the endoplasmic reticulum by a GlcNAc in a beta-1,4 linkage by POMGNT2 to generate the M3 glycans.
source: A small subset of O-Man modified sites, apparently exclusively on α-DG, are extended in the endoplasmic reticulum by a GlcNAc in a beta-1,4 linkage by POMGNT2 to generate the M3 glycans (Manzini et al., 2012; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Manzini et al., 2012 and Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013.

claim: The M3 glycan is further elaborated into a trisaccharide by the action of a beta-1,3-N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) transferase, B3GALNT2.
source: This is further elaborated into a trisaccharide by the action of a beta-1,3-N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) transferase, B3GALNT2 (Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013.

claim: POMK phosphorylates the initiating O-Man residue at the 6-position on the trisaccharide.
source: This trisaccharide is a substrate for POMK that phosphorylates the initiating O-Man residue at the 6-position (Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013.

claim: B4GAT1 adds a glucuronic acid (GlcA) in a beta-1,4 linkage to an underlying beta-linked xylose (Xyl).
source: After unknown elaboration of the phosphotrisaccharide in a phosphodiester linkage, presumably by one or more of the as-yet to be assigned CMD-causing gene products (ISPD, TMEM5, Fukutin, and FKRP), B4GAT1 adds a glucuronic acid (GlcA) in a beta-1,4 linkage to an underlying beta-linked xylose (Xyl) (Praissman et al., 2014; Willer et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Praissman et al., 2014 and Willer et al., 2014.

claim: The addition of xylose by an unspecified enzyme followed by the action of B4GAT1 serves as a primer for LARGE to synthesize the repeating Xyl-GlcA disaccharide, matriglycan, that serves as the binding site for several extracellular matrix proteins.
source: The addition of the xylose by an unspecified enzyme followed by the action of B4GAT1 serves as a primer for LARGE to synthesize the repeating Xyl-GlcA disaccharide, matriglycan, that serves as the binding site for several extracellular matrix proteins (Praissman et al., 2014; Willer et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Praissman et al., 2014 and Willer et al., 2014.

claim: A truncated, secreted version of α-DG with a COOH-terminal GFP and His tag (α–DG-340) was overexpressed in HEK293F cells and purified from the media.
source: A truncated, secreted version of α-DG with a COOH-terminal GFP and His tag (α–DG-340 that is only 28 amino acids (313–340) derived from α-DG following endogenous furin cleavage) was overexpressed in HEK293F cells, which express low levels of LARGE, and purified from the media.
evidence: The claim describes experimental procedures performed by the authors.

claim: The 28 amino acid sequence of α–DG-340 contains only one putative M3 glycan consensus site (TPT, 317–319).
source: This 28 amino acid sequence contains only one putative M3 glycan consensus site (TPT, 317–319).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis of the construct used in the study.

claim: Treatment with aqueous HF results in loss of IIH6 binding to α-DG constructs.
source: We previously demonstrated that the generation of peptides bearing the phosphotrisaccharide could be isolated from α-DG constructs following cleavage of the phoshodiester linkage and that such treatment resulted in loss of IIH6 (an antibody that binds functionally glycosylated α-DG) binding (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by prior work (Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2010) and by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tandem mass spectrometry of permethylated glycans released from α–DG-340 revealed the presence of a linear pentitol-Xyl-GlcA.
source: Tandem mass spectrometry of the permethylated glycans revealed the presence of a linear pentitol-Xyl-GlcA (Figure 2) as well as further disaccharide extended structures (pentitol-(Xyl-GlcA)n, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Further disaccharide extended structures (pentitol-(Xyl-GlcA)n) were identified in permethylated glycans released from α–DG-340.
source: Tandem mass spectrometry of the permethylated glycans revealed the presence of a linear pentitol-Xyl-GlcA (Figure 2) as well as further disaccharide extended structures (pentitol-(Xyl-GlcA)n, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ISPD is capable of generating CDP-ribitol using CTP and ribitol-5-phosphate.
source: The enzyme was capable of generating CDP-ribitol or CDP-ribose using CTP and ribitol-5-phosphate or ribose-5-phosphate, respectively, but was not able to generate the sugar (alcohol) nucleotides with ribitol or ribose (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ISPD is capable of generating CDP-ribose using CTP and ribose-5-phosphate.
source: The enzyme was capable of generating CDP-ribitol or CDP-ribose using CTP and ribitol-5-phosphate or ribose-5-phosphate, respectively, but was not able to generate the sugar (alcohol) nucleotides with ribitol or ribose (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ISPD is not able to generate CDP-ribitol or CDP-ribose with ribitol or ribose (without phosphate).
source: The enzyme was capable of generating CDP-ribitol or CDP-ribose using CTP and ribitol-5-phosphate or ribose-5-phosphate, respectively, but was not able to generate the sugar (alcohol) nucleotides with ribitol or ribose (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ISPD is a CDP-ribitol (ribose) pyrophosphorylase that generates the needed reduced sugar (alcohol) nucleotide for integration of a ribitol into the functional O-Man glycan structure.
source: Thus, ISPD is a CDP-ribitol (ribose) pyrophosphorylase that generates the needed reduced sugar (alcohol) nucleotide for integration of a ribitol into the functional O-Man glycan structure.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing ISPD's enzymatic activity.

claim: A study published during manuscript preparation demonstrated that CDP-ribose, CDP-ribitol, and CDP-ribulose could all be generated by mammalian ISPD.
source: During the preparation of our manuscript, a study was published demonstrating that CDP-ribose, CDP-ribitol, and CDP-ribulose could all be generated by mammalian ISPD consistent with our present findings (Riemersma et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Riemersma et al., 2015.

claim: Mild periodate treatment of purified α-DG-340 protein resulted in a loss of reactivity with the IIH6 antibody.
source: Thus, we performed mild periodate cleavage of the purified α-DG-340 protein and demonstrated a loss of reactivity with the IIH6 antibody that recognizes functional LARGE-modified glycoprotein (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Multiple glycopeptides were identified where Thr317 was modified to indicate a cleaved ribitol fragment on the phosphotrisaccharide.
source: We were able to identify multiple glycopeptides where Thr317 (a known site for M3 glycans) was modified to indicate a cleaved ribitol fragment on the phosphotrisaccharide.
evidence: The claim is based on tandem mass spectrometry analysis of tryptic peptides.

claim: Pairs of essentially identical glycopeptides showed cleavage between C2 and C3 or between C3 and C4 of the ribitol.
source: We observed pairs of essentially identical glycopeptides that showed cleavage between C2 and C3 or between C3 and C4 (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Peptides with an additional phosphate were observed, suggesting that there can be 2 phosphates on the trisaccharide of which at least one is in a phosphodiester linkage to ribitol.
source: We also observed peptides with an additional phosphate suggesting that there can be 2 phosphates on the trisaccharide of which at least one is in a phosphodiester linkage to ribitol (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The ribitol appears most likely to be connected at C1 to the oxygen of a phosphate group on the M3 glycopeptide and at the C5 to xylose.
source: Thus, the ribitol appears most likely to be connected at C1 to the oxygen of a phosphate group on the M3 glycopeptide and at the C5 to xylose (note that ribitol C1 and C5 are indistinguishable due to the nature of the reduced sugar and thus nomenclature for closed-ring standard sugar nucleotides is being used to describe linkage).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mass spectrometry data showing ribitol cleavage patterns.

claim: TMEM5 shows sequence similarity to glycosyltransferases.
source: Among the uncharacterized genes harboring mutations in patients with CMD, TMEM5 shows sequence similarity to glycosyltransferases (Vuillaumier-Barrot et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vuillaumier-Barrot et al., 2012.

claim: TMEM5 was among the genes uncovered in a screen for loss of IIH6 binding and Lassa virus entry.
source: TMEM5 was also among the genes uncovered in a screen for loss of IIH6 binding and Lassa virus entry, readouts that are both dependent on functional glycosylation of α-DG (Jae et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jae et al., 2013.

claim: Transmembrane deleted dTM-TMEM5 can hydrolyze UDP-Xyl, but not other UDP-sugars.
source: Using the UDP-Glo assay, we were able to show that transmembrane deleted dTM-TMEM5 can hydrolyze UDP-Xyl, but not other UDP-sugars (Figure 5A) demonstrating selective hydrolytic activity in the absence of acceptor glycans.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Recombinant full length TMEM5 can be used to label α-DG-Fc340 with radiolabeled UDP-Xyl [Xyl-14C] expressed from TMEM5-deficient patient cells compared to α-DG-Fc340 mutated at the M3 site (TPT, 317–319, converted to APA) as a negative control.
source: Furthermore, we were able to show that recombinant full length TMEM5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) can be used to label α-DG-Fc340 (Fc-tagged α-DG-340) with radiolabeled UDP-Xyl [Xyl-14C] expressed from TMEM5-deficient patient cells compared to α-DG-Fc340 mutated at the M3 site (TPT, 317–319, converted to APA) as a negative control (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: dTM-TMEM5 can use UDP-Xyl to transfer Xyl to CDP-ribitol as the acceptor but not ribitol, ribitol-5-P, or CMP-Neu5Ac.
source: Also, we were able to show that dTM-TMEM5 can use UDP-Xyl to transfer Xyl to CDP-ribitol as the acceptor but not ribitol, ribitol-5-P, or CMP-Neu5Ac suggesting the need for the ribitol to be in a phosphodiester linkage in order to be an acceptor (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: TMEM5 is the xylosyl transferase enzyme for modification of ribitol that is in a phosphodiester linkage to the M3 glycan on α-DG.
source: In summary, these results provide strong, but not direct, evidence that TMEM5 is the xylosyl transferase enzyme for modification of ribitol that is in a phosphodiester linkage to the M3 glycan on α-DG.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing TMEM5's enzymatic activity.

claim: Knockdown of tmem5 in zebrafish caused an increased percentage of embryos with mild to severe hydrocephalus (95% in total).
source: Knockdown of tmem5 caused an increased percentage of embryos with mild to severe hydrocephalus (95% in total) and significantly reduced eye size, reminiscent of pathological defects in WWS (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Knockdown of tmem5 in zebrafish caused significantly reduced eye size.
source: Knockdown of tmem5 caused an increased percentage of embryos with mild to severe hydrocephalus (95% in total) and significantly reduced eye size, reminiscent of pathological defects in WWS (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 88% of embryos co-injected with p53 and tmem5 MOs still displayed hydrocephalus and significantly reduced eye size.
source: 88% of embryos still displayed hydrocephalus and significantly reduced eye size was still observed in embryos co-injected with p53 and tmem5 MOs (Figure 6B), suggesting that the brain and eye abnormalities were not caused by MO off-target effects.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The brain and eye abnormalities in tmem5 knockdown zebrafish were not caused by MO off-target effects.
source: 88% of embryos still displayed hydrocephalus and significantly reduced eye size was still observed in embryos co-injected with p53 and tmem5 MOs (Figure 6B), suggesting that the brain and eye abnormalities were not caused by MO off-target effects.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the p53 co-injection experiment.

claim: Muscle fibers in tmem5 knockdown zebrafish were infiltrated by Evans Blue dye before undergoing degeneration.
source: Muscle fibers were infiltrated by EBD before undergoing degeneration (Figure 6C), suggesting a pathological mechanism in which knockdown of tmem5 leads to compromised sarcolemma integrity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Knockdown of tmem5 leads to compromised sarcolemma integrity.
source: Muscle fibers were infiltrated by EBD before undergoing degeneration (Figure 6C), suggesting a pathological mechanism in which knockdown of tmem5 leads to compromised sarcolemma integrity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the Evans Blue dye infiltration data.

claim: Knockdown of tmem5 in zebrafish caused a 44% reduction of glycosylated α-dystroglycan (IIH6 epitope) on Western blots.
source: Compared to control embryos, knockdown of tmem5 caused a 44% reduction of glycosylated α-dystroglycan (IIH6 epitope) on Western blots (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: TMEM5 plays a role in functional glycosylation of α-DG.
source: Together, these results clearly illustrate a role for TMEM5 in functional glycosylation of α-DG and knockdown of this enzyme generating a CMD phenotype in vertebrates.
evidence: The claim is based on the zebrafish knockdown experiments showing reduced glycosylated α-DG.

claim: Knockdown of TMEM5 generates a CMD phenotype in vertebrates.
source: Together, these results clearly illustrate a role for TMEM5 in functional glycosylation of α-DG and knockdown of this enzyme generating a CMD phenotype in vertebrates.
evidence: The claim is based on the zebrafish knockdown experiments showing hydrocephalus, reduced eye size, and muscle defects.

claim: A homozygous, non-reference c.997G>A (p.G333R) sequence variant was found in the TMEM5 gene of two affected siblings.
source: A homozygous, non-reference c.997G>A (p.G333R) sequence variant was found in the TMEM5 gene (Chr. 12) of the two affected siblings (P1 and P2), while the unaffected sibling was homozygous for the wild type sequence (c.997G, p.G333) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole exome sequencing data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The unaffected sibling was homozygous for the wild type TMEM5 sequence (c.997G, p.G333).
source: A homozygous, non-reference c.997G>A (p.G333R) sequence variant was found in the TMEM5 gene (Chr. 12) of the two affected siblings (P1 and P2), while the unaffected sibling was homozygous for the wild type sequence (c.997G, p.G333) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole exome sequencing data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The p.G333R variant was predicted to be damaging by PolyPhen-2 and SIFT.
source: The variant was predicted to be damaging by PolyPhen-2 (Adzhubei et al., 2013) and SIFT (Sim et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on computational predictions using established tools.

claim: The affected amino acid p.G333 is highly conserved and located in a functional domain predicted to have glycosyltransferase activity.
source: The highly conserved affected amino acid p.G333 is located in a functional domain that is predicted to have glycosyltransferase activity (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Two out of three pregnancies in the consanguineous family resulted in fetuses with WWS.
source: Two out of three pregnancies resulted in fetuses with WWS (P1 and P2), while the third child is normal (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on clinical observations of the family.

claim: Both WWS fetuses had classical brain developmental abnormalities detected by prenatal ultrasound.
source: Both WWS fetuses had classical brain developmental abnormalities detected by prenatal ultrasound (see Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ultrasound imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Severe dystrophic features were noted in cryosections of the muscle from the WWS patient.
source: Severe dystrophic features were noted in cryosections of the muscle, and immunofluorescence studies showed an abnormal pattern of dystrophin-glycoprotein complex expression characteristic of a severe dystroglycanopathy (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Immunofluorescence studies showed an abnormal pattern of dystrophin-glycoprotein complex expression characteristic of a severe dystroglycanopathy in the WWS patient muscle.
source: Severe dystrophic features were noted in cryosections of the muscle, and immunofluorescence studies showed an abnormal pattern of dystrophin-glycoprotein complex expression characteristic of a severe dystroglycanopathy (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Skeletal muscle from the 18 week fetus (P2) showed an α-DG glycosylation defect with complete loss of both functional glycosylation and laminin binding.
source: Immunofluorescence and western blot analysis of skeletal muscle from the 18 week fetus (P2) showed an α-DG glycosylation defect similar to previously described glycosylation-deficient WWS patients (Willer et al., 2012) with complete loss of both functional glycosylation and laminin binding (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: Expression of wildtype TMEM5 fully restored functional glycosylation in patient cells while the p.G333R mutant protein did not.
source: In the patient cells, expression of wildtype TMEM5 fully restored functional glycosylation while the p.G333R mutant protein did not (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by complementation assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Functional rescue of patient cells supports the interpretation that TMEM5 p.G333R has pathogenic relevance and causes WWS.
source: Functional rescue of patient cells supports the interpretation that TMEM5 p.G333R has pathogenic relevance and causes WWS.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the complementation assay results.

claim: Both wildtype and p.G333R TMEM5 proteins are expressed and localize to the Golgi apparatus without significant ER mislocalization.
source: Immunofluorescence and co-localization with a Golgi marker Giantin confirmed that both proteins are expressed and localize to the Golgi apparatus without significant ER mislocaliztion (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The loss of TMEM5 function in the WWS patients is not caused by a cellular processing defect, but rather directly affects the catalytic domain and abrogates the proposed xylose glycosyltransferase activity.
source: This result shows that the loss of TMEM5 function in the WWS patients is not caused by a cellular processing defect, but rather directly affects the catalytic domain and abrogates the proposed xylose glycosyltransferase activity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the localization data showing normal Golgi localization of the mutant protein.

claim: The functional M3 glycan structure on α-DG contains a phosphorylated trisaccharide extended by a ribitol in a phosphodiester linkage followed by the addition of a priming Xyl and GlcA before extension with the repeating disaccharide matriglycan by LARGE.
source: Collectively our data supports a model of a functional glycan structure on α-DG where the phosphorylated trisaccharide, which we previously identified (Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2010), is extended by a ribitol (by an unknown enzyme(s) but presumably Fukutin and/or FKRP) in a phosphodiester linkage followed by the addition of a priming Xyl (added by TMEM5) and GlcA (added by B4GAT1) before extension with the repeating disaccharide matriglycan by LARGE (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is based on integration of all experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Mutations in all of the enzymes in the functional glycan biosynthetic pathway have been demonstrated to generate secondary dystroglycanopathies in patients.
source: Mutations in all of the enzymes in this pathway have been demonstrated to generate secondary dystroglycanopathies in patients (Wells, 2013; Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015; Dobson et al., 2013; Endo, 2015; Stalnaker et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: ISPD generates CDP-ribitol for ribosylation of the phosphotrisaccharide, similar to how the DPM1/2/3 enzyme complex generates dolichol-phosphomannose for initial mannosylation.
source: Further, ISPD, similar to the DPM1/2/3 enzyme complex that generates dolichol-phosphomannose (Figure 8B) for initial mannosylation, generates CDP-ribitol (Figure 8C) for ribosylation of the phosphotrisaccharide.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing ISPD's enzymatic activity and draws an analogy to DPM1/2/3.

claim: CMD resulting from defects in ISPD and DPM1/2/3 should be referred to as tertiary dystroglycanopathies.
source: Both of these processes are involved in the generation of donors for the enzymes involved in functional glycosylation of α-DG and as such CMD resulting from these enzymes should then be referred to as tertiary dystroglycanopathies (Vuillaumier-Barrot et al., 2012; Lefeber et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the role of ISPD and DPM1/2/3 in generating sugar donors, with support from citations.

claim: Initiation and further extension of O-Man glycans on α-DG is required for proper recognition by ECM proteins.
source: Initiation and further extension of O-Man glycans on α-DG is required for proper recognition by ECM proteins (Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015; Dobson et al., 2013; Endo, 2015; Endo and Manya, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Failure of proper glycan elaboration is causal for a significant subset of congenital muscular dystrophies (CMD) referred to as dystroglycanopathies.
source: Failure of proper glycan elaboration is causal for a significant subset of congenital muscular dystrophies (CMD) referred to as dystroglycanopathies that range from severe Walker-Warburg syndrome (WWS) to the much milder Limb-Girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD) presumably resulting from the severity of the mutation on enzyme expression, stability, localization, and/or activity (Wells, 2013; Stalnaker et al., 2011; Muntoni et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The severity of dystroglycanopathies ranges from severe Walker-Warburg syndrome (WWS) to the much milder Limb-Girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD) presumably resulting from the severity of the mutation on enzyme expression, stability, localization, and/or activity.
source: Failure of proper glycan elaboration is causal for a significant subset of congenital muscular dystrophies (CMD) referred to as dystroglycanopathies that range from severe Walker-Warburg syndrome (WWS) to the much milder Limb-Girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD) presumably resulting from the severity of the mutation on enzyme expression, stability, localization, and/or activity (Wells, 2013; Stalnaker et al., 2011; Muntoni et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from clinical observations and is supported by citations.

claim: The source of ribitol-P in mammals is likely generated from ribose-5-phosphate, from the pentose phosphate pathway, by the action of aldose reductase.
source: These findings also lend themselves to considering the source of ribitol-P in mammals that likely is generated from ribose-5-phosphate, from the pentose phosphate pathway, by the action of aldose reductase (Perl et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from known metabolic pathways and is supported by a citation to Perl et al., 2011.

claim: It is possible that the reduction of ribose-phosphate to ribitol-phosphate occurs after the formation of the sugar nucleotide CDP-ribose to form CDP-ribitol.
source: Alternatively, given that ISPD can act on ribitol-phosphate and ribose-phosphate, it is possible that the reduction occurs after the formation of the sugar nucleotide CDP-ribose to form CDP-ribitol.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation that ISPD can use both substrates.

claim: No CDP-ribitol transporter into the secretory pathway has been identified yet.
source: Furthermore, no CDP-ribitol transporter into the secretory pathway has been identified yet.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of reported evidence in the literature.

claim: SLC35A1 may be a CDP-ribitol transporter.
source: Given the facts that mutations in SLC35A1, a proposed CMP-sialic acid transporter, have been implicated in decreased functional glycosylation of α-DG that is independent from sialic acid (Jae et al., 2013; Riemersma et al., 2015) and that sugar nucleotide transporters often have higher selectivity for the nucleotide than the sugar, it is inviting to speculate that SLC35A1 is a CDP-ribitol transporter though this remains to be formally tested.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from prior observations about SLC35A1 and sugar nucleotide transporter properties.

claim: Reduced and non-reduced glycans are susceptible to cleavage by mild periodate treatment between vicinal diols.
source: Both reduced and non-reduced glycans are susceptible to cleavage by mild periodate treatment between vicinal diols (Collins et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Collins et al., 1997.

claim: The M3 trisaccharide can have 2 phosphates connected directly to it (one is at the 6-position of Man and the other could not be resolved).
source: We also observed phosphotrisaccharide glycopeptides with an additional phosphate moiety suggesting that the M3 trisaccharide can have 2 phosphates connected directly to it (one is at the 6-position of Man and the other we could not resolve).
evidence: The claim is based on mass spectrometry data showing an additional phosphate.

claim: While ribitol and ribitol-5-P were not acceptors in vitro, CDP-ribitol was an acceptor for TMEM5 catalyzed transfer of Xyl from UDP-Xyl likely due to mimicking the phosphodiester linkage of the ribitol in the glycopeptide structure.
